analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers and repair shops legally bypass software locks to diagnose and repair farm equipment.
analysis.headline: The Farm Freedom to Repair Act was introduced in December 2023 and died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors and combines are controlled by embedded software that manufacturers lock down. Under current copyright law, anyone who breaks a digital lock to access that software for repairs can face legal liability, which pushes farmers back to authorized dealerships for diagnostic and repair work. This bill would change the copyright code so that bypassing these locks, for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing agricultural equipment, is legal — and so that making or selling the tools that do it is legal too. The bill never moved: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and independent repair shops. Farmers gain the legal right to fix their own tractors and combines or hire any shop, instead of waiting on authorized dealers — often at harvest time when a day of downtime is costly. Independent mechanics and repair-tool makers gain a legal market for diagnostic software and repair tools. Buyers of used farm equipment also gain, since the right to repair supports resale value.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of digital farm equipment from the copyright law's ban on circumventing technological protection measures, so farmers and shops who unlock their own equipment cannot be sued for it [S2].
Also exempts making, importing, or selling the tools, software, and devices used to bypass the locks, which would let an independent repair market function [S2].

Defines covered equipment as 'any agricultural product dependent, in whole or in part, upon attached or embedded digital electronics to function' — a broad sweep covering most modern farm machinery [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers that currently channel diagnostic and repair work through authorized dealers. Repair fees, diagnostic fees, and dealer markups are a profitable, recurring part of their business model, and independent repair competes with it. Some manufacturers also argue that opening software access raises safety, emissions-control, and warranty questions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks

drawbacks.text: Copyright exclusions carve out an exception to software protections rather than imposing a general repair obligation; manufacturers can still design around it, control parts availability, and restrict physical access, so the bill addresses the legal barrier but not every practical one.

Manufacturers argue wider access to vehicle software raises safety, emissions tampering, and intellectual-property concerns; this is the standard good-faith objection to right-to-repair measures, though the bill limits the exemption to repair purposes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to farmers are concrete and immediate: fewer trips to a distant dealer, less downtime during planting and harvest, and lower repair bills. The costs to the public are essentially nil; the cost falls on a concentrated industry that currently captures repair revenue through exclusive control of software access. Safety and emissions concerns are the strongest objection, but the bill's purpose limitation (repair only) is a reasonable answer to it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; it never got a hearing, never left committee, and died when the Congress ended [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the Farm Freedom to Repair Act on December 19, 2023 [S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — the committee with jurisdiction over copyright law [S4].
The bill attracted no cosponsors [S3] and no further action appears in its history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers kept exclusive control over the diagnostics and repair of the machines they sell. Farmers are left paying dealership rates for repairs and bearing downtime while waiting for authorized service.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment makers and their dealer networks

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2023 and sponsored it; she recruited no cosponsors.

for.name: Farmers and right-to-repair advocates
for.what_they_did: Advocated for legislation allowing farmers to fix their own software-controlled equipment; no advocacy action tied to this specific bill appears in the record.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee without a vote.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers (e.g., John Deere and similar makers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair mandates that would open their software to independent repair; no specific lobbying action on this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan divide ever took shape; the fatal obstacle was inaction, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: These companies sell machines controlled by proprietary software and steer diagnosis and repair through their own dealer networks, capturing a recurring stream of service revenue. The bill would allow any farmer or shop to bypass the software locks, opening that market to competition. Their interest in keeping repairs exclusive runs against farmers' interest in cheap, fast fixes.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and third-party tool makers
industries.note: The bill would legalize selling diagnostic and repair tools for modern farm equipment, creating a market that copyright law currently chills. Every farmer who gains the right to repair gains a place to exercise it.
Dealers capture service work because farmers cannot legally bypass software locks to diagnose problems themselves. Independent competition would take some of that work and its margins.
